At 6:17 in the morning, the city is undecided.

It has not yet become itself. The streets are too empty to be called busy, but not empty enough to be peaceful. A delivery truck groans at the corner. Somewhere behind a row of dark windows, a coffee machine begins its daily labor with a low mechanical shudder. The sky is the color of an unwashed plate, and the buildings wait without expression.

I like this hour because it belongs to no one. Night has not entirely released it, and morning has not yet claimed it. The people who are awake are mostly moving for practical reasons: hospital workers, bakers, cleaners, taxi drivers, parents whose children have developed a mysterious relationship with dawn. Their lives are already in motion, but the rest of the world is still gathering itself.

There is a particular dignity in being awake before the day has made demands.

At 6:17, a person can stand beside a window and pretend that life is simple. There is the cup, the chair, the faintly glowing rectangle of the phone, the refrigerator humming like a distant engine. The mind has not yet opened all its drawers. It has not remembered the unfinished email, the awkward conversation, the appointment, the bill, the thing said three years ago that still occasionally rises from the depths to ask whether it was embarrassing. Morning gives us a brief amnesty from ourselves.

Then the light changes.

It does not arrive dramatically. No trumpet sounds. The sky simply becomes less gray. The edges of things sharpen. A tree across the street reveals its branches, which were present all along but hidden by the darkness. The world is not created by daylight, exactly; it is confessed by it.

This seems true of people as well. We are never entirely what we appear to be in any one moment. A quiet person may be holding an entire argument inside them. A cheerful person may be carrying a private sorrow with the care of someone transporting a bowl filled to the brim. A stranger who cuts in front of you at the grocery store may have just received bad news, or may simply be inconsiderate. We rarely know which. Every person is a room with the lights off.

The older I get, the more suspicious I become of quick judgments. They are efficient, but efficiency is not the same as wisdom. It is tempting to divide the world into generous and selfish, brave and cowardly, interesting and dull. These categories make life easier to navigate. They also make it smaller. People are inconsistent creatures. We can be kind in one hour and cruel in the next, courageous in public and frightened in private. We can love someone deeply and still fail them in ordinary ways.

Perhaps maturity is not becoming better than this, but becoming more honest about it.

A friend once told me that every person has a private museum. I have thought about that ever since. In this museum are objects no one else would understand: a ticket stub, a broken toy, a postcard with a faded stamp, a shirt worn on a day that mattered for reasons invisible to everyone else. There are rooms devoted to people who are no longer in our lives. Some rooms are bright and carefully maintained. Others are locked.

Sometimes, without warning, we find ourselves standing in one of those rooms.

A song can do it. So can the smell of wet pavement, the particular blue of evening, or the sound of someone laughing in a way that resembles a person we once loved. Memory is not an orderly archive. It is more like a house whose doors open when they please. We do not retrieve the past so much as trip over it.

This is inconvenient, but perhaps it is also a gift. The past does not disappear simply because time moves forward. It changes shape. A childhood fear may become a source of tenderness. An old humiliation may become a story. A loss may remain a loss while also becoming evidence that something mattered.

We often speak of healing as though it means returning to an earlier version of ourselves, untouched and complete. But no one returns. The scar is part of the map. Healing, if it happens, is more like learning the geography of a changed country. You discover where the roads are damaged, where the rivers run differently, where you can build.

Outside, the city is waking now. The bakery lights have come on. A cyclist passes in a yellow jacket, bright as a moving flame. A woman in a dark coat pauses at the crosswalk and looks up at the sky, perhaps checking the weather, perhaps simply looking. For one second, everyone is connected by the same pale morning: the cyclist, the woman, the baker, the unseen person washing a cup in an apartment above the street.

Then the traffic light changes, and the spell breaks.

This is the strange bargain of being alive. We are given moments of unity, but they are brief. We spend most of our time inside separate bodies, carrying separate histories, unable to fully enter one another’s experience. Yet we keep trying. We tell stories. We make jokes. We cook meals for people who are tired. We send messages that say, in various forms, I thought of you. We place flowers on graves. We ask questions and sometimes listen to the answers.

These gestures may look small against the enormous machinery of the world. They are small. But smallness is not the same as insignificance.

A hand on a shoulder can alter the direction of an afternoon. A sentence can remain in someone’s mind for decades. A stranger who holds the elevator door may become, for a moment, proof that the world is not entirely indifferent. We rarely know which of our actions will matter. The kind word we forget may be remembered by someone else. The careless remark we barely notice may become part of a wound.

This is why attention matters. To pay attention is to admit that the world is real. The cracked mug, the tired cashier, the sparrow shaking rain from its feathers, the old man carefully folding a newspaper—none of these things are background. They are events. They are occurring once, and then never again in precisely the same way.

At 6:17 tomorrow morning, the city will be undecided again. The same streets will wait, though not exactly as they waited today. Someone will wake with a new worry. Someone else will wake relieved. A child will lose a tooth. A dog will bark at a delivery truck. Somewhere, perhaps, a person who has been lonely for a long time will receive an unexpected message and stare at it before answering.

The day will begin, as days do, without explaining itself.

And we will enter it carrying our private museums, our unfinished thoughts, our ordinary hopes. We will make mistakes. We will be generous. We will forget what we meant to remember and remember what we meant to forget. We will move through the hours, sometimes awake to them, sometimes not.

Still, the light will come.

It will reveal the branches, the windows, the faces. It will show us the world as it is—not simple, not finished, not safe from sorrow, but present.

For now, that is enough.
